utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The case is here today for a hearing on the motions for judgement of acquittal made by the accused Mr. Kordic, represented by myself today; and by Mr. Turner Smith, to my left; and also by the accused Mr. Cerkez. Both motions are made pursuant to Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. We have read the very extensive proceedings, particularly on your behalf, in the case; we have read the motion more succinct on behalf of Mr. Cerkez; and we have read the Prosecution response, and so what we would like to hear from you is any comment you have on the Prosecution response and deal with any matters which we want to raise. There is no need to go over all the matters in the original pleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What I had planned to do, Mr. President, in fact, I prepared an outline of the argument that we have prepared to make today, which I'd like to distribute, if I may. If the Court has any particular questions on the items that we want to zero in on, I'd be more than happy to respond, and I will say that as I understand the Prosecution's brief, the Prosecution expressly states that they do not intend to respond point by point to the arguments made by Mr. Kordic specifically. In fact, there is no detailed response to the recitation of the evidence that we included with as much care as we possibly could in the submissions that we made to the Court. As I understand it, basically the Prosecution articulates, in the first 20 or so pages of their brief, their view of the applicable standard of review of motions made pursuant to Rule 98 bis, and we will address that. They then essentially go on to recite the allegations made in the amended indictment. There's a brief summary of the Prosecution's view of the evidence against Mr. Kordic, and a rather more elaborate and detailed summary of the evidence against Mr. Cerkez. But as I understand it, the Prosecution stated they had no intent to make any detailed response to our brief, saving that, rather, for today. So if I may, Your Honour, I'd just like to distribute an outline of the argument and explain to you who from our side will be doing what, and we'll try to be as succinct as possible, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me make the point again. There is no need to repeat what's in your pleading. You can answer what the Prosecution have said, but we don't want to hear constant repetition. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And bearing that in mind, Your Honour, although I have prepared a very extensive oral argument today, let me just touch briefly upon the points in a succinct manner as possible. Let me just start by saying obviously there is a mountain of evidence in this case, but I hope we've shown the Trial Chamber that very little of it is of any specificity against Mr. Kordic. And we are mindful of the magnitude of the pleadings that we have filed, and we apologise for their length, but the seven-day requirement of Rule 98 bis imposes significant obligations upon Defence counsel in a case of this sort, and I apologise for transferring those obligations to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution, but to quote Blaise Pascal: "Unfortunately, we did not have time to make the submission any shorter." As we see it, the two essential theories that are articulated in the amended indictment and which are addressed by the evidence are a theory of command responsibility under Section 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute, and I will handle any questions the Court has on that particular subject with the exception of the standard of review, which I will touch on very lightly and give Mr. Kordic's view, and if the Court has any detailed questions on the standard of review, although it seems rather uncontroversial, Mr. Smith will address those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The standard of review is uncontroversial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Extremely controversial, I would have thought, judging by your pleadings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In our view, Your Honour, the leading case on the application on the Rule 98 bis, which was existed only since November 30th last year, is the Jelisic case, which is consigned to a footnote in the Prosecution's submission. The reason we would respectfully submit to the Trial Chamber that the standard of review is uncontroversial is because the standard is outlined in paragraph 108 of the Jelisic case in black and white. Let me just recite that. The Court said in paragraph 108: "All things considered, the Prosecution has not established beyond all reasonable doubt the charge of genocide made against Goran Jelisic in connection with the crimes in the detention camp at Brcko." The Court said: "The Trial Chamber therefore concludes that it has not been proved beyond all reasonable doubt." And this was on, by the way, a motion for judgement -- actually, it was a consideration of Rule 98 bis issue made ex proprio motu by the Trial Chamber, not upon application by the accused in that case. The Court said: "It has not been proved beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused was motivated by the dolus specialis of the crime of genocide. The benefit of the doubt must always go to the accused. Consequently, Goran Jelisic must be found not guilty on this count."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause there. Now, that was a case in which the Trial Chamber were about to acquit Jelisic, which is what they did. Now, of course, that is open to us here. But what we are doing is considering, at this stage of the case, what is the test that we have to apply in reviewing the evidence. And you will see there is an extensive recitation of authority in the Prosecution brief dealing with national authority, and also the other cases, Celebici and Tadic, in this Tribunal. Now, what we have to determine is whether there is sufficient evidence to support a conviction. That means to sustain a conviction; evidence which is adequate for that purpose. Now, you will tell me if I'm wrong, but it looks as though the wording in the Rule came from the United States federal rules, which seems to be the only jurisdiction in which the sort of test which you say should be applied is applied. In all other jurisdictions, and indeed in Tadic and Celebici, both cases, of course, before Rule 98 bis, but the Trial Chambers in those cases, and in other jurisdictions, apply what may be thought to be the usual test at this stage, which is: Is there evidence on which a reasonable Tribunal, properly directing itself as to the law, could convict? It's not a question of establishing burdens of proof and that sort of thing. It's a question of looking, as a matter of law, to see whether there is the evidence upon any charge on which a Tribunal, as I say, a reasonable Tribunal, could convict. Now, the test which you postulate and which was applied in Jelisic is the test which is applied at the end of a case, when you are reviewing all the evidence, and our Trial Chamber is reviewing all the evidence, deciding what weight to give it, and then deciding whether the case is proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Now, that is a plausible reading of the law. Some would say it is the correct reading of the law. But that's the argument that you've got to deal with. And you may like to consider this proposition: If your submissions are right, it would mean that the Trial Chamber, if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, would have to convict at this stage, which would mean that the Defence would have to call evidence and would have to call evidence on every point. And that doesn't seem to me to be part of the adversarial system. And what you have done is to transpose the final test and try and make it a test to be applied at this stage. That, as I say, is a reading of the law, which some might find convincing. So, far from being uncontroversial, it may be it's your submission which is controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. It may be that our submission is controversial, but the only decision I believe to interpret Rule 98 bis to date is the Jelisic decision, and the Jelisic decision articulates the Rule, which is the basis of our submission. The reason that I said it was uncontroversial is precisely because that was the standard that was adopted in Jelisic. And we had not anticipated that there would be such an extensive challenge to that particular proposition. But let me just say, Mr. Smith is prepared to address the detailed issue presented by Rule 98 bis and the standard of review. I'll turn the podium over to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The argument that we present on Rule 98 bis and its standard is predicated on several propositions. The first is that the Prosecution has the burden, and the entire burden from the outset, of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. And it has the obligation as it presents its case and before it rests its case to prove, to present evidence that proves guilt in its judgement beyond a reasonable doubt. In other words, it does the best job it can. And once it has rested its case, that is, as far as the evidence the Prosecution has chosen to lead, as good as it gets. That's the high-water mark, if you like, of the Prosecution's case. And the defendant, because of the burden to go forward and present a case by the Prosecution, has no obligation to present a case himself, he has a right to present that case should, in his judgement, the Prosecution get beyond the goal line, if you like, in presenting his case. Now, the Rule that looks to the reasonable court test was developed originally in the context of jury trials, both in the United States and in the United Kingdom. Indeed, the Galbraith decision is a jury case. In that situation, the person making the decision at the end of the Prosecution case is not the ultimate trier of fact and thus is not empowered, if you like, at that stage to withdraw the case from a jury unless it is satisfied that no reasonable juror could conclude that the person was guilty, the defendant or the accused was guilty. Now, the Prosecution cites -- let me back off a moment. In the United Kingdom, a commentator, Archbold, has recognised that where the judge himself is the ultimate trier of fact and there is no jury or other party who will normally make the decision on the facts, that in that situation, the judge should, logic compels, judicial efficiency compels, that the judge not ask himself at that stage what he would do at the end of the case. The Prosecution has made its best case, and the judge judges on the basis of that case. In the United States, the Prosecution has presented one old District Court opinion, that the normal jury rule, which is much discussed, because generally accused have required juries in the United States, has also been applied in the context where there is just a trial to the judge, and it is our argument that the logic of the rule is wholly lacking when the judge himself, or the Judges in this case, are the ultimate triers of fact, and that judicial efficiency is far better served for the judges to decide, when the Prosecution has taken its best shot, whether the case needs to go forward; in effect, whether this should be the end of the case. Now, we have interpreted that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If as in Jelisic the Trial Chamber come to that conclusion, then, of course, they then have to apply the reasonable doubt test. They have to say, if they're going to stop the case altogether, that they are satisfied that the Prosecution have not satisfied them beyond reasonable doubt. It is, if you like, the ultimate test, using that expression. But here where -- for the sake of argument, let us say there is some evidence on a particular count -- the issue is whether, if there is some evidence, the Tribunal should at this stage decide whether they convict on the count or not, and that is what I suggest is the wrong or may be the wrong question. There may be circumstances where the evidence is so totally discredited or so totally unreliable that a Trial Chamber could feel that it could not rely on it, or there may be cases where there is simply no evidence at all or it's insufficient to carry the inference which the Prosecution invite a Trial Chamber to draw, and it may be that in those extreme cases that a Trial Chamber should direct an acquittal at this stage, but it would then have to ask itself that question. But overall, the question is: Is there evidence on which the Trial Chamber could convict? It's a question of what the Trial Chamber has to ask itself. I might just add this: that from my knowledge, although you're right about Galbraith and the way that that test was developed in the context of the jury system, there is, certainly in England, a system, as you may know, of magistrates who sit in courts of three and are the judges of law and of fact, and as far as they're concerned, the test in a practice direction is whether there is evidence on which a reasonable court could convict. So although of course one also has to have regard to the jury context, it's not always the case that it makes a major distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I would start, in dealing with that, by saying that it seems to me there cannot and should not be two standards under Rule 98 bis. Rule 98 bis operates at the end of the Prosecutor's case on two actuating mechanisms. One is the motion of the accused, and the other is the option of the Judges proprio motu which was the situation in Jelisic. It seems to me, in any case, that if the Judges had themselves the opportunity to acquit the defendant if they did not believe the evidence sufficient on a reasonable-doubt test, that the accused has necessarily, by implication, to have the opportunity to attempt to persuade the judges of that conclusion. In the United Kingdom case, I'm not familiar, not being from that jurisdiction, with the ins and the outs, but I had thought that it was indeed the summary proceedings before a magistrate situation that Archbold was addressing, and the Prosecution just pointed out that there is at least a case undercutting the conclusion that Archbold reaches, but I submit to you that the logic of what he has said is what drives his conclusion and our argument, and that logic is driven also by judicial efficiency. If the judges can see, when the Prosecution has taken its best shot, that it did not present enough evidence to convict, then judicial efficiency is served by dealing with the case right then. The Defence has a right to proceed and put on additional evidence. It seems to me the Defence is not under any duty, because it is always the Prosecution which bears the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. And the Prosecution has taken its shot at doing that and has rested its case, and it has no opportunity to put on additional evidence except in rebuttal to what the Defence presents in its case. It seems -- we had interpreted it indeed, and one of the reasons we thought this was uncontroversial, we had seen the use of the reasonable judge standard in the Celebici and Tadic cases, and then we had then seen the Tribunal enact Rule 98 bis, with language that we thought, because it dealt with the close of the Prosecution case, the Trial Chamber finding insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction and being required, shall order entry of judgement of acquittal. We had interpreted Rule 98 bis, possibly in error, as being a considered view by this International Tribunal, which is not bound by the both corpus of jurisprudence and perhaps, we submit in this case, mistakes in the context of the judge as an alternate trier of fact of the law of national jurisdictions. We had thought that was what the Tribunal was doing, and we thought it wise and exactly the right decision. And I should point out that in the civil law context, in the common law context, I pointed to this issue of the fact that there is no jury here. There is no other person to decide. In the civil law context, pointed to by the Prosecution, the decisions made before the Trial Judge takes the case are made by persons other than the Trial Judge. And at that stage in the civil proceeding, any person making a decision, in effect, in place of the Trial Judge, must apply or may logically apply a standard that is not simply making a decision on the merits. And once the trial commences in a civil proceeding, it is simply structured differently than it is both at common law and here in this adversarial process. There is no -- the judge takes command. The judge tries the case. There is no Prosecution puts on its case, makes the best case it can, and then we see whether it is necessary for judicial resources, and the resources of the defendant, to be employed further in the process. And that at base -- our argument is based on logic, on what we see as a misperception and misapplication of a jury-based rule, with judge as ultimate trier of fact context. And the fact that this Tribunal is an International Tribunal, stands at the threshold, needs the assistance of judicial efficiency. And we think, based on the Rule as enacted, if the Judges may consider and dismiss an indictment, then the Defence has to be given the opportunity to make that argument. And that is what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are entitled, of course, to make the arguments, but it's a question of what test the Court has to apply. And if you are right in saying that the Chamber should order the entry of judgement of acquittal, if it finds that a case is not proved beyond reasonable doubt, then, presumably, the Rule would have said that. There is a distinction between what the Trial Chamber said in Jelisic, when it said it wasn't satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, that was its finding, and the question which a Trial Chamber necessarily has to ask itself, or you ask the Trial Chamber to find, namely, that in each case it has to go through the indictment and satisfy itself at this stage that the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt. It's not what the Rule says. And it doesn't necessarily follow from the finding in Jelisic that that's what the Trial Chamber should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to the Defence that the issue involved in the interpretation of Rule 98 bis is whether there is a good reason for the trial to go forward, if the Trial Chamber can see, based on the evidence, the best case the Prosecution can put on and they have then rested, that it needs to do so. Now, that involves some greater work for the Trial Chamber mid-case than otherwise, and the Prosecution has pointed this out. But in the long-term interests of efficiency, it seems to me -- particularly given the length of these trials and the period of Pre-Trial detention that these prisoners, these accused suffer in coming to trial, that long-term efficiency is far more greatly served by the Trial Chamber looking carefully at the evidence at this stage and asking itself, since it is the ultimate trier of fact, it need not hypothesise what someone else would do, if it sees that the Prosecution has failed, and we believe the Prosecution has, and have said so, then it seems to us this is the appropriate time to end the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I was fascinated by your formulation on "good reason." It depends on what you mean by "good reason." I think I would accept "good reason" if by that you mean that there is evidence which raises the legal possibility of conviction, as distinct from the certainty of conviction. Good reason, I think, doesn't mean much more than some reason, some lawful reason. You have been referred to the system of trials by magistrates, who are triers both of law and fact in some jurisdictions. It has happened in some jurisdictions where that system applies that a magistrate will rule that there is a case to answer. The Defence calls no evidence whatsoever, and the magistrate acquits. The magistrate acquits because he is applying, at the end of the case, a totally different standard from the standard which he applies at the halfway stage. At the end of the case, he applies a standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt. At the midway stage he is applying the lower standard of what I call the legal possibility as distinct from the certainty of conviction. I doubt whether the test of proof beyond reasonable doubt is one that would inure to the benefit of the accused. Because if the ruling were to be made on that basis, surely it would be very difficult thereafter to secure an acquittal. Either very difficult or -- either impossible or very difficult to secure an acquittal thereafter. I don't believe that that was what was intended at all. I will agree that the formulation of Rule 98 bis is perhaps not as apposite as it might have been; that it might be open to the interpretation that you give it. But I think when you read it against the background, when you read it against the background of the travaux, the history, I think it is clear that it is addressing the situation at the halfway stage, and not the situation at the end of the case. And that the applicable standard, therefore, could not be the standard which is applied at the end of the case. I think that would give rise to interminable difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may address some of those points as well as I may. On the question of whether it puts the Defence in an untenable position. I would too have the test applied at this stage. I would suggest that the Defence always, as a practical matter, but not as a matter of law, of duty, has an obligation to put on a case, and to assume that the Prosecution has gotten over the goal line, when it has rested its case. It would be entirely imprudent for a defendant to make any other assumption; very risky for a defendant to make any other assumption. And a formulation that, in the absence of a jury or other decision-maker, does not require the Trial Chamber now to test the Prosecution's case rested, made it its best, in our judgement relieves, in a sense, the Prosecution of the burden of making the best case it can the first time around, before it closes its case. Again a question of efficiency. And it furthermore throws on the Defence a burden of going forward to put on a case when, in our judgement, it should not have to do so; in a case in which, if the Trial Chamber were to focus, it would have concluded that the Defence was made -- rather, that the Prosecution has not proved guilt beyond a reasonable doubt now. And it does not so focus. It forces the Defence to spend additional resources to go through a trial, judicial resources to be expended in a situation in which the Defence should have no burden to go forward. Or it should have only the right to oppose the Prosecution, but it is always on the Prosecution to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and in an adversary system, that opportunity is at the beginning of the trial before the Prosecution rests. Because after they have rested, their only right is to rebut matters brought forward by the accused. And our submission is that as an International Court you are free from the corpus, to reconsider the corpus of law, and should do so and make your judgements about what you think is most efficient and what you think is the fairest procedure, considering the obligations on the Prosecution and the rights of a defendant, and judicial efficiency, given the type of cases you face and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, all that we would accept, of course. And certainly we have in mind the length of the case and our powers in relation to it, and the fact that it's an international tribunal. But we still have to apply the practical law. If you are right, as Judge Robinson points out, the effect of what you are doing would be that at halftime in a case you would have the trier -- Trial Chamber, if ruling against the Defence, effectively ruling for a conviction. You therefore remove the opportunity of submitting, as you would in front of the magistrate that Judge Robinson mentioned, submitting at the end of the case: Well, there is some evidence, but it doesn't amount to anything, and therefore you can't be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt. You have removed that possibility, because you've had the Trial Chamber rule at half-time that they are satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt. So you would effectively remove that argument from the Defence. You would also put the Defence, as I said earlier, in the position of having to call evidence if it wanted to secure an acquittal. Now, is that, really, if you think about it, in the Defence -- the accused's interests to be boxed in in that way? Because that's the effect of your test if we were to apply it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would answer that two ways. The first is that you may have removed the opportunity at the end of the case of moving for a judgement based solely on the Prosecution evidence, but you gave the Defence that opportunity when the Prosecution's evidence had closed. And at the end of the case, the Defence will generally have put in additional evidence, perhaps with rebuttal evidence, and it is then a different question, because the Judges are looking at a different corpus of evidence. So while you remove the opportunity at the end of the case to test solely only the basis of the Prosecution's evidence, you have given it to the Defence at the time it should be given, as a matter of efficiency, when the Prosecution has rested and done its best. Secondly, as to the question whether there is detriment to the Defence because there is an implicit decision, after the Prosecution's requested if the Defence fails under our test, that the evidence at that stage is sufficient to convict, you've given the Defence the opportunity to test it, and the Defence has the right to put on additional evidence. And if the Defence makes a request and it fails, you can be very certain that the Defence will indeed put on additional evidence because it will know, implicitly, that it must do so. I see no disadvantage to the Defence when you give it the right to test to the Prosecution's case once the Prosecution has taken its best shot, and then the Defence has the right to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless anybody else has a point. Yes, Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smith, one last question to you, please. I am not from a common-law culture, so I will speak from a rather different point of view. As you have said, we are here, part of an international tribunal, and as members of such a tribunal, we have to take into account the different sources of law which we might use in order to establish our general principles of function, but we are an international tribunal, and as you have said, we are not linked by one system, rather, by another, and we are not either bound by the decisions taken by another Trial Chamber. Let me add that in passing. The only thing that interests us is to know whether or not the Appeals Chamber has given any decision which might be of application in our particular trial or may be useful as a decision to turn towards when need arises. But there is something that bothers me somewhat, and maybe it is something that arises from the very way Rule 98 bis is written. Rule 98 bis and the Jelisic decision do not say that the evidence put forward are not sufficient to declare the culpability of the accused. They say they can justify condemnation -- a conviction, sustain a conviction. There was something that was said by Mr. Cerkez's Defence counsel in order to explain this expression of “sustain a conviction”. What does it mean to sustain a conviction? It means something that can be at the very basis of a possible conviction. And if it is something that can sustain a possible conviction, it means that there is some evidence that has been presented that have enabled the Judges to go beyond the prima facie test, elements of proof, evidence that can be used as a reasonable basis for a possible conviction, which is not to say that at this particular stage of the procedure, that we find ourselves in the position that allows ourselves to give to the evidence its true weight. Are we able, at this stage, to determine whether or not that element of proof or that evidence is indeed one that has to be considered? You have the problem of the evidence, and then you have the problem of the indicia of reliability that you can attribute to that evidence. Of course there is some evidence, but that's not enough. You have to further analyse the evidence submitted to you. Is this evidence enough to lead someone to say that an accused will be convicted beyond all reasonable doubt? And that is the ultimate test, the ultimate phase. Why is that so? Well, because in all conscience, in order to come to what is called in other legal systems, in order to convince one's self intimately of the guilt of an accused, you have to have all the elements, and that includes the evidence presented by the Defence. Only then can you establish proof. Only then can you attribute to the various evidence their true weight and estimate their reliability. Now, of course you will tell us, but in the adversarial system there is cross-examination of the witnesses, and by cross-examination you have gathered a number of elements and information, but we have not gathered all the information we need, and this idea of proof beyond a reasonable doubt implies that we have all the information, all the data between our hands, and that is the reason for which the system provides for the Defence the possibility of taking the floor once the Prosecution has put its case forward and has tried to justify its allegations. The Defence is allowed to give its interpretation of the facts. This is the reason why what Judge Robinson says to you is so interesting. The test to be applied midway through the trial is not to be applied at the end of the trial. Up to now, I haven't heard you tell us in what way there is a difference between the test that you wish us to apply midway through and the test that would be applied at the end of the procedure when there should be a difference. Otherwise, the adversarial system, which we're mentioning in this debate, would not be satisfactorily constructed. It would not be a reasonable system. If you can apply the same test midway through the trial and at the end of the trial, then one wonders what good it is to go to the very end of the trial. At the end of the trial, one is supposed to benefit from additional information, from additional data which enables one to give better weight to the evidence, elements which one does not benefit from midway through the trial. Now, in some legal systems, you have this idea of prima facie. This is something that all international legal specialists know of, and there have been a lot of decisions taken, among others, by the International Court of Justice, which explained this prima facie test. So in that particular sense, I do accept that the evidence, as submitted, has to go beyond the prima facie test in order for the Tribunal to take a decision on the basis of Rule 98 bis. However, this is not something that you can apply to the very end. That does not interfere with the fact that you have to prove facts beyond reasonable doubt, and this test of proof beyond reasonable doubt marks the very end of the process. Prima facie marks the beginning of the process. Proof beyond reasonable doubt marks the end of the process and the possible conviction of the accused. But in between, you have to find a particular test to apply, and this is at the very core of our argument today. This is what I mean to tell you, Mr. Smith. This is what my reactions are to your arguments, and maybe you have some additional remarks you would wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, let me see if I can shed light on my views. Take the prima facie test initially. There is a prima facie test established in the Statute, Article 9, section 1, for the confirmation of an indictment. I would argue that that test must be at least as stringent as the reasonable court test, reasonable Trial Chamber test, because it should not be possible to confirm an indictment on the basis of facts on which a reasonable Trial Chamber could not convict a person, and it is on that basis that it seems to me that is the stage at which this is the relevant question. Now, let me address also the reasonable Trial Chamber test itself. That test has three very important characteristics. First, the question asked necessarily is: Could a reasonable Trial Chamber convict under a beyond the reasonable doubt test? So the beyond reasonable doubt test is built in necessarily, even to the test the Trial Chamber would apply at this stage, even under the theory argued by the Prosecution. Secondly, under that very same test, evidence must be weighed. Its credibility must be weighed, because, of course, what is at issue is whether a reasonable Trial Chamber could convict on the basis of the evidence, and to make that judgement, you must consider credibility and weight in the question of whether they could convict under the beyond a reasonable doubt test. Third, having then formulated those first two propositions in that way, there is no place at all for arbitratory presumptions. Having formulated the test as what a reasonable Trial Chamber would do, you have built the deference into the standard from the outset, and there is, therefore, no place for artificial presumptions in favour of the Prosecution, et cetera. So that, in effect, many of the difficulties you consider you face with the rule we propose, I submit you face already applying a reasonable Trial Chamber standard at this point in time. Now, on the question of midpoint versus end point, and whether we are talking about the same test. We are talking about the same test, because always the guilt of the accused must be judged under the same test. And the point here is, and the essential point, I think it goes absolutely to the heart of the issue, in an adversary proceeding where the Prosecution has the burden of proving in guilt, entire burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the half point of an adversary proceeding can and should be in proper cases the end point. And it is fundamentally different from a non-adversary, civil law procedure in which a judge simply says to himself: I want to listen to all of the evidence, and I will direct the proceeding. And I want all the evidence in front of me. In an adversary process, all of the evidence the Prosecution is entitled to present is in front of the judges when they rest their case. That is at the very heart of the adversary process. The Prosecution has that burden. And that burden cannot and should not be shifted to the defendant where there is no reason for doing it. And where there is no jury, where the judge, the same judge making the decision now will make the decision at the end of the case, there is no good reason or rationale. And in our judgement, the long-term judicial efficiency argues very strongly in testing the Prosecution's case when they have finished and rested, in putting forth their case. That is their opportunity, to put on evidence about the guilt of the accused. And after that they have no right, other than one of rebuttal. And the judge is in a fundamentally different position than in a non-adversary proceeding. And I will be glad to answer any further questions, Your Honour, but, in short, those are the reasons why we have argued the position we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I think what would be most helpful now is this: I've seen the outline of the argument. It seems to me that it covers a great deal of the material which is already in the brief, and it won't be of great assistance, but of course we'll hear what argument you have. But let us not waste too much time going over old matter. What I think we would find to be -- what would be of assistance is dealing with any counts on which you say there is no evidence at all, if there are any, or on which you say the evidence is not sufficient, as the rule says, to convict. We'll move away from the test for the moment. If you'll deal with the factual elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take it that the Trial Chamber does not want to hear a rearticulation of our views or our submissions relating to the principles of superior responsibility or command responsibility under Section 7(3), and that's fine. I think we've outlined those fully in our brief, and there doesn't appear to be too much point in going over them, other than to emphasise just this one point. And that is that the general principles, I think, are outlined in the Celebici case. And the Court there stresses the importance of taking great caution, when principles of superior responsibility, or command responsibility, are stretched beyond the normal confines of that doctrine, which is in the context of the military chain of command. Where you have military superiors, military subordinates, that's the context in which the test was generated, and that's the context in which it's most appropriately applied. With respect to civilian alleged superiors, though, very difficult questions are posed. And the Celebici case makes it clear that the doctrine can extend to civilian superiors, but only to the extent that they exercise a degree of control over their subordinates that is similar to that of military commanders. And I cite paragraph 389 of the Celebici diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed the Court there stressed that great care had to be taken, lest an injustice be committed, in holding individuals responsible for the acts of others in situations where the link of control is absent or too remote. It's the link of control that the Celebici case appropriately emphasises. Just to respond very briefly to one of the issues raised by the Prosecution in this regard, Your Honour, or Your Honours. The Prosecution cites to a decision from the Rwanda Tribunal in the Kayishema and Ruzindena case, saying that -- this is page 30 of the Prosecution's brief: Powers of influence are sufficient to impose superior responsibility. That's it, says the Prosecution. If you are a man of influence, of whatever undefined nature, that's enough to make you potentially responsible under Section 6(3) of the Rwanda Statute, which is the analog of Section 7(3) of this Tribunal's Statute. But we submit that the Kayishema case was very careful to make clear the circumstances in which superior responsibility applies to civilians. In paragraph 216 of the Kayishema decision, the Trial Chamber there said: "The crucial question is not the civilian status of the accused, but of the degree of authority he exercised over his subordinates." And in paragraph 222, the Court says it's really a test of effective control, and then concludes with paragraph 229 on this note: "The principle of command responsibility must only apply to those superiors who exercise effective control over their subordinates. The material ability to control the actions of subordinates is the touchstone of individual responsibility under Article 6(3) of the Rwanda Statute." We think, without belabouring all of the extensive discussion concerning the principles of superior responsibility, that that really is the focus of the question that the Court must ask itself: Has the Prosecution in this case proven a case of superior responsibility under Section 7(3) under whatever standard the Trial Chamber decides is the appropriate standard to apply under Rule 98 bis? I will also point out that there is one gloss on this rule that comes from the Aleksovski case, and that is that -- in connection with the Aleksovski Trial Chamber's observation, that a superior's powers to impose punishment may not necessarily be essential in considering whether a case of superior responsibility has been made out. And this was in the -- obviously in the context of a prison commandant. The Aleksovski case says we must also consider the possibility that reports may be sufficient to provoke an investigation, reports to the appropriate authorities, and that the superior may be expected, under the appropriate circumstances, to report crimes up the chain, if you like, of his chain of civilian command to the appropriate authorities, which will in all likelihood trigger an investigation that might ultimately result in the imposition of disciplinary or criminal measures or punishment. But the context in which that case was decided was not one where infractions or crimes were known to the appropriate authorities. And it was the obligation of the defendant Aleksovski in that case to stop the process by making reports up either to the military or the civilian chain of command. It's not applicable to a situation where investigations are already underway. And I just say that as an introduction to specifically the Ahmici allegations and the Stupni Do allegations, where it is clear that investigations were initiated by the HVO authorities. And I'll address those in just a second. I was going to go into the separation of military authorities from civilian institutions. I recall very clearly, Mr. President, you asked me a question during Sir Martin Garrod's cross-examination on the question of the testimony that he had given regarding intertwining of military and civilian institutions. And the question that was posed to me was: Was it conceded that there was an intertwining throughout the period of the amended indictment of military and civilian institutions? And the response that I gave was it was not conceded because it's not a fact. It's absolutely clear that the -- after the declaration of an imminent state of a threat of war by the RBiH on April the 8th of 1992, the entire country was in a state of confusion; the Croat political and military authorities were in a complete state of confusion. There was no distinct Croat -- Bosnian Croat military. The political institutions and the military institutions were all mixed up into one. And I think Dr. Ribicic was helpful in explaining precisely how the Bosnian Croats slowly organised themselves over the succeeding seven months or so. And he identified two particular points in time. The first was July the 3rd, of 1992, when the HZ HB authorities met. They passed a number of decrees. This was the first time that a decree on the armed forces was passed. But it's also significant that the -- there was an amended decision relating to the basic composition of the HZ HB which created, the Trial Chamber will recall, the office of president. The president, of course, was the supreme commander of the armed forces under Article 29. That was the point at which the civilian authorities started to separate from the military authorities, and that was a process that continued over the course of the next few months. And it reached its epiphany in October, on October the 17th of 1992, after all of the institutions of the HVO government had been established, the Prime Minister had been appointed, the president of the HVO government, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, all of the departments were established, including the Department of Defence. And detailed roles of military discipline had been adopted, the district military Prosecutor's office had been established. And Dr. Ribicic conceded, as he had to, that at that time the civilian government had established its organs and was operating. And the military institutions had been established and were appropriately governed and made subject to a separate code of disciplinary procedures. And I think the evidence is absolutely clear from the Prosecution's own evidence that the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was established and fully operational under Colonel Blaskic's dominion by November the 11th, 1992, as we stated in our brief. By that time, it's absolutely clear that the civilian and the military institutions had separated. And I think that's important, when you take a look at the evidence of the chain of command in this case, a subject which we repeatedly revisited in cross-examination, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, Mr. Sayers, but we must have some regard to the clock. This is a matter which you rehearsed extensively in your brief. Unless there is a particular point in response to the Prosecution, I think you can take it that we have your submissions on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. There is only one point that I would like to make or add in respect to our position that Mr. Kordic was not in the military chain of command. We think that the evidence is virtually uncontroverted that he was not in the chain of command. And the only evidence, and I'll address this particularly when we get to the claims made regarding Busovaca in January of 1993, the only evidence that puts Mr. Kordic specifically in a military chain of command is just -- is purely opinion evidence. And it comes from Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart. And he gave an opinion to the effect that Mr. Kordic, I believe, was the military commander in Busovaca, based upon a meeting that he had had with Mr. Kordic on February the 3rd of 1993. But we also would like to address the Court's attention to Brigadier Duncan's testimony on this subject. He stated, on page 10465 of his testimony: "As for Blaskic's status as commander, it was quite clear to me he was very much the commander," and he articulated why. "He had a large headquarters, well-equipped staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need to go over that again. I think we have those submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I'll pass to the particular crimes section. I think that's what you've addressed my attention to, Mr. President. Are there any charges upon which there is absolutely no evidence, is the inquiry. Yes. Count 1 makes a claim of -- a generalised claim of persecution throughout the HZ HB/HR HB and the municipality of Zenica in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, I'll defer to Mr. Smith, who's going to be handling the persecution claims made in Count 1, but if I may, just by way of brief introduction, say this: The amended indictment specifically charges that the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, consisted initially of 30, 3-0 municipalities and then one additional municipality, Zepca, was added subsequently to the founding of the HZ HB on November the 18th, 1991. As to 24 of those municipalities, there is quite simply no evidence of any persecution: Jajce, Skender Vakuf, Kakanj, Kotor Varos, Tomislavgrad, to name just a few. Insofar as other municipalities are concerned, let me touch upon the following: Travnik. There is no evidence of any persecution of Bosnian Muslims by Bosnian Croats in Travnik, Mr. President, and the other Judges of the Trial Chamber. Major Hay, and Colonel Morsink from BritBat and the ECMM basically covered the entire area from April through October of 1993 and neither of them ever saw Mr. Kordic in Travnik. The only evidence of a particular problem in Travnik occurs on April the 12th, 1993, when some flags, I believe, were raised, or April the 8th to the 12th when flags were raised in Travnik, and they were promptly torn down by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and set on fire and then there was a fight that followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, are you dealing with the specific issue or is Mr. Smith going to deal with this, because I would prefer to hear the listing of the 24 municipalities, the specific counts in which you say there is no evidence, so that when the Prosecution comes to reply, they can reply specifically to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you just give us the counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The only municipalities as to which evidence has been put on, I think, are these: Travnik municipality; Kresevo, through Witness E; Fojnica, through witness Stjepan Tuka; and then the principal municipalities that are concerned in the amended indictment, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Zepca, Vares, and Kiseljak. As to all other municipalities that were in the HZ HB, there is no evidence. Therefore, we would submit to the Trial Chamber that to the extent that the amended indictment asserts that there was a persecution case made out in those 24 municipalities as to which no evidence has been put on, then those claims have to be dismissed at this stage. As I say, I'll leave the specifics to Mr. Smith, but let me just address three particular municipalities, if I may, Travnik, Kresevo, and Fojnica. I've already made the points that I wanted to make with respect to Travnik. Let me just add to that that according to the testimony of Witness AA, he was called to address the particular problems that occurred in the outbreak of fighting on April the 12th, and the person with whom he dealt was not Mr. Kordic at all but, rather, Mr. Valenta. Insofar as the claims of persecution are made regarding Travnik, they would appear to be completely misplaced in view of the overwhelming, indeed uncontroverted evidence of persecution going the other way with the June 8th offensive launched by the ABiH that resulted in not only 20.000 displaced persons, according to the testimony of Witness AD, but also atrocities in Maljina, Cukle, and Mileticic, according to the evidence of Mr. Bower. Turning to Kresevo, there is no evidence connecting Mr. Kordic to any of the events in Kresevo, Your Honours. No one suggests that he had anything to do with any of the events there and, indeed, Witness E never saw Mr. Kordic in Kresevo at any time, and testified that as far as he was aware, he was the vice-president of the HDZ and that's all; no military capacity whatsoever. But that's the only evidence, I believe I'm correct in saying, presented by the Prosecution relating to Kresevo through Witness E. And in connection with the municipality of Fojnica, there are no crimes alleged, I believe, against Muslims before Muslims launched their surprise offensive on July 2nd, 1993. In fact, the evidence shows that if there was persecution and discrimination, it was discriminations by Bosnian Muslims against Bosnian Croats in that jurisdiction. And I would simply refer the Court's attention to the October the 10th, 1993 special report prepared by the ECMM that states precisely that. It's Exhibit 2201/1 at tab 10. Seven thousand people were expelled from their homes, all Bosnian Croats. Only about 150 were left in the municipality. Persecution and discrimination was noted in the report, along with the destruction of Croat villages and the looting and pillaging of Croat houses, but no evidence or no allegations of crimes against Muslims in the municipality, and certainly, of course, no evidence that Mr. Kordic would have had anything to do with such crimes even if there were such, because he was only seen there, according to Mr. Tuka, once, at a soccer game. And with that, with the Court's permission, unless it has any questions for me, I'll just hand over the persecution theory to Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Let me address first but very briefly the Article 7(1) questions, and I would remind Your Honours or urge that on 7(1), as elsewhere, criminal laws must be narrowly construed, and that in considering the question of nullum crimen sine lege, one must consider the interpretation one is giving to the law, not just the question of whether murder was obviously a crime in 1991 or 1992. The question is: Did the accused have a fair notice of the types of interpretations now being made on, as it is said, aetiological or from purposive analysis basis, in US parlance, as you are considering the law to apply? Also there are three situations involved in this case that give reason for care. First, one is dealing with theories of indirect liability; secondly, one is dealing in most cases with circumstantial evidence and inferences; and thirdly, one is dealing, in most cases, in many cases, with hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to interrupt you, Mr. Smith. If I've understood you well -- I'm listening to you in English, so I'm not always sure I've got you right -- are you basically telling us that the principle of nullum crimen sine lege means that not only the rule exists before the perpetration of a crime but also that the interpretation of the rule can only be applied in a rather narrow sense, at the moment the crime is perpetrated. You speak of the rule but also the interpretation of the rule. You mentioned this particular rule of the law but also the interpretation of this rule of the law, and you tell us that the interpretation that is made of this rule is the one that is in application at the moment when the crime is committed. Is that what you're telling? Because that being the case, I would ask for more explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have spoken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to follow your logic and your line of thought, because I'm not following right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed, and that is entirely my fault, Your Honour. What I intended to say was that in applying the rule of nullum crimen sine lege, one must apply it not only to questions as to substantive law, as to whether this substantive law was the law at the time when the action took place in 1992, 1993, 1994, but one must also consider that same principle when considering the expansive interpretations of an existing law that was in effect at that time, that one is now, at a later time, making or engaging in. I'm saying the question of notice, given the lack of maturity, if you like, of the substantive humanitarian and criminal law being applied by this Tribunal for the first time since World War II, as it is working out the principles, giving them flesh, giving them rationales and reason and extruding from the basic propositions what the law really is and really means, you must have firmly in mind the question of the notice to the accused that the law in that form and as so interpreted would have been apparent to him had, in the middle of a civil war, had chosen and had the opportunity to consult a lawyer prior to taking his actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, now, how does this relate to whether there's a sufficiency of relevance under Rule 98 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, the sufficiency of the evidence must be tested against the applicable substantive law, and we have argued the applicable substantive law as to Article 7(1), 7(3) in our prior trial briefs, as to Articles 2, 3, and 5. So that in order to make a determination about the sufficiency of the evidence, you must have in mind some view of the law to which you are applying the evidence. We have argued and the Prosecution has argued about the applicable law, and I'm simply articulating a general principle that I think needs to be borne in mind when you consider the legal issues. Let me, as to 7(1), say only further that it is our view that all of the offences charged under 7(1) fail to come up even to a reasonable Trial Chamber test insofar as sufficiency of the evidence is concerned, but I am not now making an argument that there is no evidence at all insofar as they are concerned. Let me turn to prosecution -- persecution, sorry, and make four simple points. The first relates to the law to be applied on the question of mens rea, and it is the mens rea point that we have raised in this motion at this stage. The definition of mens rea for persecution stems, in effect, from the definition of a discriminatory act found in the Kupreskic Trial Chamber, and must be uppermost in Your Honours' minds. That mens rea requirement, as is said there, is higher than that for ordinary crimes against humanity, and the inquiry is whether the evidence in this case shows beyond a reasonable doubt a desire to deprive a defined group of its fundamental rights -- and I'll come back to this in a moment -- as laid down in international customary or treaty law so as to remove the persons in that group from the society in which they live or even from humanity itself. That, in our judgement, is a very high standard indeed. Let me deal then with three points raised in the Prosecution brief on the question of persecution. First, relating to the question whether Mr. Kordic ever personally discriminated. The Prosecution in its brief mentions a comment related by the witness -- a witness that Mr. Kordic had at one point said that -- had uttered the phrase "culturally inferior Muslim culture." And it is this point that I raised the definition in particular about fundamental rights and removing persons from society in which they live and humanity itself. I think, if I were to ask most Europeans whether they thought American culture was culturally inferior to European culture, virtually to a man and a woman, they would say it was. And I submit to Your Honours that this is not the sort of -- has not the sort of gravatus that one needs in terms of evidence of persecutory intent. In addition to that comment, there were two other issues raised in the Prosecution brief. One is that the accused referred in his public remarks to Mujahedin and Muslim extremists. And I would submit to Your Honours that on the record of this case, that constitutes a simple statement of fact. The third point that was raised within this general setting of whether the defendant personally discriminated, is his articulation of a political concern about the development or the danger of an Islamist state in Bosnia. And I mention again that as one is dealing with issues of speech and with issues of political speech and political association, one is in a very delicate area. I simply refer Your Honours to the remarks by a Muslim member of the BiH presidency that were played on a videotape for Your Honours, in which Mr. Durakovic said that he was aware that the presidency of the BiH, the figures there, and he was a member of that, a Muslim member, were only figureheads. That the presidency is not where the real decisions were made, and it was not the real decision centre of power. The real decisions, he said, relevant to military questions, were made independently within a smaller staff headed by the president. And I quote now: "When things became a lot worse, when an almost ethnically pure BiH army was being established, when religion began to be used for political purposes, when they purged the BiH army of so-called inappropriate individuals, people who were not members of the Party of Democratic Action, people who did not use a shalom greeting, and people who did not try to present themselves falsely as new religious people, we sent ..." This is a member of the presidency speaking, a Muslim member. "... we sent that famous letter signed by five members of the presidency in which we expressed our opinions about the politicisation of the army and the instrumentalisation of the religion for political purposes." So again I would simply say that these statements about political concerns for the nature of the way in which the Bosnian government and its state was developing, and as to Mujahedin and Muslim extremists, are not unjustified in political discourse on the basis of this record. Now, the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you come to that point, it's time for an adjournment. The other point may be this. That, of course, one could look at an accused's statements or matters attributed to him to determine whether there is an intent, a persecutory intent, but one can also, it may be said, infer an intent from the actions of an accused, depending on what they are. But we'll return. I would be grateful if you could, Mr. Smith, Mr. Sayers, have in mind the clock. We want to hear the submissions today, if at all possible, and Mr. Cerkez's counsel, and also the Prosecution, must have time to reply by this afternoon. Very well. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have pending, I think, a question about inferences from what the defendant did on the question of discriminatory intent. That is directly to the point. In dealing with persecution and the related issue of instigation, there are really three simple inquiries: What did the accused do; what did the accused say; and did the accused encourage anyone by what he did or said? We have addressed the question of inferences from what the accused did in our brief. And I would point Your Honour to a discussion of a period, 1991 and early 1992, and the story of the political exercises going on in the HDZ-BiH as it led up to the referendum. Secondly, we have discussed what the defendant did in participating in the creation and execution of Bosnian Croat institutions. That part of the brief we have addressed the question of whether there is any de jure discrimination in those institutions, and whether there is any de facto discrimination from the conduct involved during that period with those institutions. We, on de facto, have addressed the meeting of the municipalities on September 22, 1992; the second General Assembly of the HDZ BiH on December 14th; and the alleged ultimatums in the spring of 1993, the winter and spring of 1993. Finally, in terms of the conduct of the accused, we have addressed the question of participation generally in the civil war between the Muslim community and the Croat community. I will not go over those, only simply point you to those parts of the brief, and end this part of -- first part of my discussion of persecution by noting that on -- that deals with the question of what he did as Your Honour has raised, but there is simply no proof there, and there is no proof as to what he said and what he encouraged anyone to do of any evidence of persecution; simply no statements in which he is beating on the table, taking intemperate positions not appropriate in their context, in blaming people. He is calmly considering. If you will read the videotape material that we have quoted in the brief, the excerpt we have placed in the annex, we have tried to place the accused's own words in front of the Trial Chamber so that you may make your own decisions. There is, of course, hearsay evidence, not corroborated, that other things were said. The best example there, I think, is Witness AQ, who when questioned said no. The press conference for which we have the transcript and for which Your Honours know exactly what the accused said, that was the source of her recollections of a rather more embroidered version of what he said. Let me then pass on to the second issue I wish to address concerning matters raised in the Prosecution brief related to persecution, and that is this notion that they advance in relation to the meeting on December 27th in Zagreb with President Tudjman, that there was an expectation arising from that meeting that there would be objections by the Muslim community to the course of action, negotiation for option 3 as a political choice that President Tudjman articulated there. I might first note that we have argued, and I believe in their brief at 62, the Prosecution effectively concedes that whatever you think about the discussion at that 27 December meeting, there were no instructions to use force to accomplish the objectives settled upon. There was, rather, a political decision and direction to negotiate both with the Serbs and with the Muslim community over the question of demarcation, as it is put there. And, of course, there were people who said that the Muslims may object. There was, therefore, from that point of view, an expectation of objection. Any time one goes into a negotiation, one expects the other side may object, but that's what a negotiation is all about. That's what makes a negotiation. You don't pull your punch and not make your point and argue your case in a negotiation simply because there may be an objection. And there were, as the Prosecution concedes, no instructions to use force. Indeed, negotiations were had. The negotiations did not succeed. The Bosnian Croats were then faced with the need for deciding whether to vote for independence with a referendum question that did not resolve, before that vote as they wished, the question of the internal organisation and constitutional structure of the new nation and which did not give them protection, in advance, of the traditional constituent and sovereign rights that they enjoyed as a nation, as that term is used in Yugoslav constitutional law. And what did they do? They did not opt out the way the Serbs did and act by force. They negotiated as hard as they could. They posed the Livno question. They tried to persuade the Muslim community to accept that formulation of the referendum question. They failed again, and they finally decided, when the chips were down, to vote. They did vote, and it is those votes and only those votes that carried the referendum to the level necessary for the independence of BiH. And as for the defendant, he had his political say at that point on various issues. When the decision was made politically, he signed the petition in Busovaca, along with his wife and neighbours, in favour of a sovereign BiH. The referendum then passed, and partition or annexation was a dead letter after that point. Now, the third issue I'd like to deal with is the argument by the Prosecution that the Bosnian Croat institutions constituted monoethnic entities with monoethnic policy, in a way discriminatory against the Muslim community. First point, of course, is these were temporary wartime institutions, not intended to last beyond a transition to peacetime entities. They were legitimate forms of self-organisation for survival and created out of necessity. We've argued that in the brief and I won't go further on it. I think it is most useful simply to recite the conclusions of the Prosecution's own expert witness, who concluded, when asked whether there had been discriminatory legislation by the Bosnian Croat institutions, no, or very few explicitly discriminatory provisions in the HZ HB enactments. I also point to the April 8th, 1992 founding decision on the military HVO, which expressly provided for the protection of all people, not simply the Croats. And Dr. Ribicic conceded this. I mentioned also that citizens were defined under the law being developed and applied in the HZ HB as citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not citizens of Herceg-Bosna, not citizens of Croatia, reflecting again always the intent that these institutions function within the entity BiH, sovereign BiH. And there was a decree on the treatment of foreigners during time of war, in which all citizens of BiH were treated equally. He agreed, Dr. Ribicic did, that any citizen of BiH could be a judge in the court system, and indeed that there likely were judges as there were, who were Muslim. He said that -- he conceded that during the second General Assembly in Mostar on November 14th, Mr. Boban himself said that the HZ HB is the state not only of the Croats who live there but every other people as well, and the question of the plight of the Muslims was raised there, and we quote that material in our brief. Dr. Ribicic also agreed that there was a long list of very specific human rights articulated and enacted by the HR HB at that stage in the evolution and development of the government institutions. That was, in effect, the same list found in the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, because, of course, the HR HB was intended to implement, as an internal republic, the proposals in that plan. Finally, Dr. Ribicic conceded that the founding decision of the HR HB itself provided that the authority in the republic was derived from the people as a community of free and equal citizens, not solely from the Croat people. Your Honour, it seems to us, and we submit, that while there may have been in the leadership a predominance of Croats in the HZ HB, that to take a situation in which there is an entity with the leadership of a particular political persuasion or racial persuasion or religious persuasion or even, although it's not listed in the Statute, ethnic persuasion, and to argue from that, even though there were other members of other -- members of other groups involved at various levels, either in this case in the military or in the administration -- in our brief, for example, in Busovaca, articulates exactly how many Muslims were in the administration all the way up through December of 1992. To argue that that is a monoethnic entity and is somehow depriving other groups of their rights is, in effect, like arguing that when in the United States the democratic administration takes over, and a lot of the top jobs are then allocated to democrats, or in the UK when one party takes over the parliament and thus takes over the government but other people are still involved at various levels, that those organisations are not monoethnic, and that in the context of temporary wartime conditions, total chaos, people trying to organise themselves to deal with the very basic necessities of safety and security for their families and reaching out, as we have shown in our brief, to the Muslim community, that when negotiations, for example, in Busovaca, in the summer of 1992, after the Kaonik barracks incident in which the Croats were reaching out to the Muslim community in the surrounding municipalities, and the Croats repeated -- they got started, they repeated their invitations, and at some point the Muslim representatives were instructed to cease dealing with the Croats. I would simply suggest to you that in context the actions of these institutions, and of the thousands of people who in good faith entered into them and worked in them, as did the accused, Mr. Kordic, this is not discriminatory or persecutory action. This is self-organisation, defensive action, coping with a very difficult reality, not of their own making. And for the reasons I articulated, de jure, de facto, the way these institutions actually operated, they did a remarkable job, under the circumstances, in trying to deal with the tensions and difficulties between groups, as groups in time of danger tend each to circle the wagon amongst people they know. And I turn the podium back over briefly to my colleague, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, just going back to Count 1, and your submission in relation to the 24 municipalities. What Count 1 refers to, paragraph 36, refers to widespread systematic persecutions of Bosnian Muslim civilians, et cetera, throughout the HZ HB. And you identify -- you say eight municipalities on which there was possibly some evidence, although you question whether there is any evidence, about Fojnica. But given that the count is worded in the way that it is throughout the HZ HB, and in the absence of any -- in the absence of any application to amend the indictment, how would you ask us to proceed, even if we were -- even if we thought you were right, there was something in your submission that there was no evidence about the other municipalities. In practical terms, how is that to be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, that's, if I may say, an excellent question. And it's something that puts us in something of a quandary, if I may say so, Mr. President, because, unless the Court declares that there is no evidence with respect to the 24 municipalities that have not been the subject of any evidence at all, unless the Court declares that we are not required to put on any evidence with respect to them, the Court can well see that the scope of our case is virtually unbounded. I mean, we've got an allegation here of crimes throughout all of these municipalities, and unless the Court says: Well, we only have evidence as to, for example, nine of them, you don't have to put on evidence with respect to the others, then we are going to have to do that. And I would suggest that that would exactly be an appropriate function of this motion for judgement of acquittal at this stage of the case. For the Court to say, or to use it, if you will, as a tool to tell us what the Trial Chamber sees as genuinely in dispute in this case, and what is not. Because if we can have -- well, I mean, I think the point is obvious. If we have to put on evidence with respect to all of those municipalities, we are looking at a considerable amount of evidence. If we don't, then we can do what we have previously articulated to the Trial Chamber we hoped to do, and put on a streamlined case that's directed to the specific points that the Trial Chamber considers to be genuinely in dispute as having been made out by whatever standard the Trial Chamber considers is applicable on this -- on this motion. Now, with respect to Travnik, we would submit there is no evidence of persecution against Bosnian Muslims by Bosnian Croats, but also no connection that Mr. Kordic has with anything that went on in Travnik. And the witnesses testimony, and the documents in this case establish that, we think, beyond apparent venture of a doubt. The same is true of Kresevo and the same is true of Fojnica. We do concede that the evidence is concentrated upon the six municipalities that I enumerated. And with the Trial Chamber's permission, I would like to turn to those six municipalities, if I may, to identify what we see as being the points that are really in dispute, and those which are not. Let me just use as an example an evocative example -- an evocative subject. The subject of Ahmici. There isn't any question that crimes occurred in Ahmici, and we've never contended that there is any argument that crimes did not occur there. They did. The point is: Did Mr. Kordic have any connection with them? And I'll argue in just a second, if the Court permits me, that there isn't. The same is true, even more so, with respect to the crimes that occurred in Stupni Do, which are gone into at great length in our brief. But just to touch upon a few subjects before I get into those more weighty ones. For example, the allegations regarding Rotilj. The Prosecution has put on some evidence that there were some people killed there. The Prosecution has put on some evidence that there were people interned there. But the Prosecution hasn't put on any evidence that Mr. Kordic had anything to do with those events, even if they could be considered to be crimes. In fact, the testimony of Witness AD, and I think it's pretty much uncontroverted, is that one couldn't even travel from Busovaca to the Kiseljak municipality where Rotilj is located after the ABiH had established hegemony over the main supply route from Kacuni to Bilalovac. And the evidence is absolutely uncontroverted that that occurred on January the 20th. It's in a milinfosum that's recorded on that same day contemporaneously. And every witness has agreed that the ABiH had effectively insulated the Vitez-Busovaca enclave or pocket from the Kiseljak pocket, and there simply is nothing to connect anything that went on in Rotilj with Mr. Kordic. And just one other point of detail on that. The evidence put on from Colonel Morsink establishes that Rotilj was actually defended. In fact, he interviewed the HVO commander who had led the assault, Mirko Redzo, and testified to that at page 8219 of the transcript. He testified that he was told that fire was returned from the village by ABiH units there, one of his soldiers was wounded. And he testified at 8221, he had no reason to doubt Redzo's story. And indeed the civilians that he interviewed in the village thereafter didn't contest Mr. Redzo's story either. So with respect to the allegations regarding Rotilj, there is nothing to connect Mr. Kordic with any of them. And the same is true of another discrete incident which has received quite a bit of attention. Tulica in counts 7 through 13, and 37 through 39. The Trial Chamber will recall from the maps that Tulica is at the southern-most tip of the Kiseljak pocket, and, in fact, right on the front lines with the Bosnian-Serb army. To use the precise phraseology of Section 7(3), Your Honours, there is no proof in this case, no evidence at all, that Mr. Kordic knew of the events at Tulica or had reason to know of the events that had occurred there. But more importantly, and we would just rely upon the testimony of Brigadier Winfield Hayes for this particular point, he being the chief of staff of UNPROFOR, having his headquarters in Kiseljak, spending six months there, and that six months encompassed the time of the fighting in Tulica and in the Kiseljak municipality generally, he was asked whether he ever saw Mr. Kordic there, and he said no. He was asked whether Mr. Kordic had any influence in Kiseljak at all, as far as he was aware, and he said no. And he certainly wouldn't go to Mr. Kordic to resolve any short-term or even long-term problem that arose in the municipality of Kiseljak. So in the absence of knowledge of the crimes that had occurred in Tulica or a reason to know, to recite the language of Section 7(3) of the Tribunal Statute, there couldn't be any allegation of superior responsibility in the sense of a failure to punish, I think, under the facts of this case, even if Mr. Kordic had any kind of military power to punish the combatants who engaged in the Tulica operation. And the evidence is absolutely clear that he did not. In fact, the evidence is replete with examples of Colonel Blaskic imposing disciplinary sanctions. The last witness who testified in this case gave an example of that himself, when Colonel Blaskic imposed a five per cent pay penalty upon the 4th battalion of military police for disciplinary infractions generally. And he also gave particular examples of the operation of the military discipline, Your Honours.
