Is that what you mean when you say yes, but persecution is linked to everything else in the counts, in the different counts, when you speak of persecution, but also killings, destruction of a certain number of religious buildings, et cetera? Could you be a little more specific? What do you mean by the crime of persecution? What is your definition of such a crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour's question to me is susceptible to the simple answer yes, yes in both parts. First as to our adoption of the proposition postulated by His Honour Judge May that these can be matters of inference; but second, in answer to Your Honour's more specific question: Yes, of course, the campaign of persecutions carried out through, as the indictment alleges, attacking cities, towns, villages, and civilians, killing and causing injury to Muslim civilians and so on, makes it quite clear that the persecution count incorporates all or most of the other matters referred to elsewhere. It is, in a sense, the overarching, or in another sense, the central allegation made. As we know from the jurisprudence on accumulative charging here, there is, in the Tribunal, there is nothing wrong with and everything right with these matters being charged the way that they have been, but yes, but it incorporates the evidence that relates to the other counts. The couple of examples I was just going to touch to, in case the Chamber had forgotten them, was Cicak, Kljuic, and Tuka being forced out of their positions by reasons of intolerance in the same way -- we had an example, I think, of a Croat Colonel in the ABiH, if you remember, who couldn't be spoken to, was untouchable. Now, when we turn from the generalities as to the evidence going to show the existence of the persecution campaign, which I don't intend to deal with any more, it's set out in Annex 1, in any event, to Kordic's involvement, again this is covered fully in our brief, his involvement in all of this campaign, in the entire area, is established in various ways but simply and shortly because he is shown to be the man with authority and power is set out in our brief. He never denied the authority and power when it was sought of him. He was regarded by all as the most important person in the territory. It's clear on all accounts that the military are driven by politicians, probably in nearly all or all wars, but certainly in this particular territory with its particular communist history. There is plenty more detailed material to which we could take you in respect of authority beyond that that is referred to in our brief, which was necessarily prepared at some short notice and ignorant of what might be argued as no case, true no-case examples. I am loathe to take too much time, looking at the clock, but I can certainly identify, in case it's helpful, the particular additional exhibits that you may want to look at, if you are at all concerned about the state of the evidence on this. The Chamber will, of course, have in mind the transcripts of the meeting with President Tudjman, 23773.1, where he was present, and the capacity in which he was present, representing that entire community. It will have in mind 219 of the 19th of September of 1992, where his signature authorised somebody to carry military equipment from one territory to another. It will have in mind Z128, where the defendant Kordic signs for the Central Bosnia regional command allowing free passage of individual -- sorry. The exhibit reference I gave first is wrong. It should be 2717. Z128, an example of his having the power by signature, and I think over a Mostar seal, to authorise someone to carry arms in the territory. Z187, ordering a meeting at Grude and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We are getting the French coming through on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises for this technical mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We are on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Z139, giving an order to Vares, which of course is always important in relation to Vares and Stupni Do, to allow unimpeded access to the HVO of the Ilidza municipality, signing as deputy president of HZ HB. 187, a further compulsory attendance invitation to the president of Vares, HVO. Z202, the handwritten note from Rajic requesting people to report to Kordic for financial allowances. 219, an order signed by Blaskic in respect of weapons going towards Herzegovina requiring a valid stamp of either the regional staff or the main command with the signature of Kordic, or Blaskic. The Court will want to have in mind Z233, a document on the 22nd of September signed by Kordic dealing with the complete control of the HVO of the Vares municipality and various other matters, signed in his capacity as deputy president of the HVO. Z229, 30th of September 1992, a note of a meeting where Kordic was speaking for the entire Croat people and saying that if negotiations with the Muslims didn't take place, then the Croats must engage in total obstruction. And he appeared to chair and take over the meeting, although not listed as its chairman. He spoke of a meeting the previous day in Vares, Z261, an order signed by Rajic on the 29th of October, stating that Dario Kordic as deputy commander of HZ HB requested he send all available forces to defend Jajce. 2624.1, a meeting where Colonel Kordic is signed as being present. Z1080, I needn't trouble with that, I think, and various other documents. So in addition to the material that we've summarised towards the end of our submission, the case against Mr. Kordic, as the Chamber will well have recognised, is that on the evidence he is shown to be the most important person and is and was the most important person in that area, plainly having authority over military matters. An aside. Complaint is made of the fact that these people, the international witnesses who were there to preserve the peace, didn't ask him very often what his power was. Strange for them to be criticised for that, but never mind. Odd for them to be criticised for that. When you see a man who travels with armed outriders in another car, who can only be approached at his distant and well-armed location by passing through layers of armed men, as we've been told, and a man who never denies his authority, nothing could be less surprising. It's hardly the case that they are going to go to such a man, in his retreat outside Busovaca, and ask him if he is, in reality, the press spokesman. One can think of a number of examples of people who simply don't need to be enquired of as to their function. Even in courts, I suppose you can. Authority is revealed by what people do and, in his case, by his never denying that he had it, and by showing, by the things that he did, that he had it. The Defence for Kordic then turn to deal with various towns, for example, Travnik and Fojnica, which aren't specified in the indictment and therefore to which I don't need to turn. Villages like Rotilj and locations like Tulica. Now, if I am right in saying that the indictments in principle stand and aren't to be interfered with at this stage for absence of evidence about a particular location, then I don't need to deal with the evidence about those particular villages. Out of respect for the arguments advanced, I'll say a few things, just perhaps to correct some misapprehensions that the Chamber might otherwise have. As to Rotilj being a defendant place, the position there, I think from the Morsink testimony, was that the HVO commander concerned had explained that one of his patrols had come under fire, and one of his soldiers had been hit. But that's within the overall setting of seven people found dead, including women, of 20 houses burnt. There is further evidence that the Chamber may find in, I think, Exhibit 702, in the order from Blaskic on the 17th of April, setting out that there was to be the capture of the areas that included that village. As to Zepce, there is quite a lot that I could say, but again it's possibly not necessary to deal with it in that much detail. But in addition to what we've said in our brief generally, the Chamber will want to remind itself, perhaps, that in the evidence of Stutt at 15159 in the transcript and Exhibit 1293.2, you heard about the defendant Kordic speaking graphically of Boban's heart being in Central Bosnia, and saying in terms that the HVO would fight to the last man to defend the pockets of Kiseljak, Kresevo, and Zepce, an area in which he was plainly, the Court may decide, interested. In the evidence of Witness AD, and with reference to Exhibit 1176.2, there was further reference to -- by Kordic to the suggestion that the HVO would regain territory they had lost, and link the Kiseljak, Vares, and Zepce pockets. Sir Martin Garrod, at 13539, dealing with Exhibit 1364.6, spoke of the defendant saying that the Muslims wanted the Lasva Valley, Zepce, Kiseljak, and other locations. Witness D, at page 3421 in the transcript, deals with some of the crime base in Zepce. The Chamber will remember that probably for the number of prisoners involved, 1.500 in the hangar, matters of that sort, and the suspicion that there were 5.000, and the percentage of the parts of Zepce inhabited by Muslims that had been destroyed. You also are hearing evidence of the appalling conditions in which people were detained. You heard evidence of the destructions of mosques in Zepce and so on. So Zepce is a place in respect of which Kordic had a clear interest. It fell within the territory in which he had an interest, and of which, as we say in our brief, he was not just an operator, he was a creator. He was in at the beginning. This was his enterprise. As to Zenica, Your Honour has correctly said that Zenica features both in the attack and in the persecutions. But I do not take it that it is being said as to the evidence of the shelling that there is no evidence. The arguments that have all been addressed, have all been arguments as to weight. On that topic, I could, if the Chamber would want it, or if I judge that I ought to, go into the evidence in some detail. Perhaps it's sufficient to note this, because the Defence rely on the conclusion, or appear to rely on the conclusion in Blaskic. In Blaskic, the evidence was either probable or very probable that it was established with the HVO, but not beyond reasonable doubt. And that was at the end of all the evidence, different from the evidence in this case. It was after hearing an expert who may or may not be called in this case. And, of course, that finding alone shows that there would be evidence sufficient to meet whatever test is judged appropriate at the half-time in a trial like this. The Chamber will have in mind, in relation to Zenica, evidence that may not have been available in the Blaskic case, including the tape-recording between Blaskic -- the tape-recording of the telephone conversation between Blaskic and Kordic includes, I think it's at page 2, Kordic expressing his views on shelling Zenica at that much earlier -- not much earlier, that earlier time, saying, "Well, if they fight back, we'll shell them, but not now." A tape-recording of very considerable value in all particulars going to show his authority, his position vis-a-vis Blaskic, but also going to show an interest at that stage in shelling Zenica. Also, and I am not sure if this evidence was available in this form in Blaskic. You have the evidence not only of where the shells came from, and the probable location within the territory of the HVO, you have the phone call to the radio station before, and the very clear evidence from the expert Hamill, that what was shown as happening in those three shells was an absolutely standard target and hit by somebody being kept informed of where the first shell was landing, moving to the position that it sought to reach, namely, the radio station. Something that may have been judged a target, by no means a proper military target, and so on. I only go into it in that limited degree of detail to emphasise the point that Zenica, even if it's separable in any way within any of these counts in the indictment, which we challenge, is something for which there is plentiful evidence at this stage, different evidence from the evidence in Blaskic, and evidence, of course, to go forward to final determination. In addition on Zenica, you've had some evidence from a witness. I'm not sure if he was protected or not so I better not name him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have to attend a meeting at 4, between 4 and 4.15. If you'd like to go on till 4, we'll then rise. We'll sit again at 4.15 until 5, with a view to finishing these submissions today, which would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should think that would be possible. I hope so. I'm sorry, I haven't checked whether he was protected or not. It was a protected witness who gave evidence, effectively, of reverse ethnic cleansing in Zenica, he being a Muslim taken to Krizancevo Selo, used as a hostage, and where there was efforts made for him -- where he wanted to go to Zenica with his family, that could only be accomplished on terms of the removal of Croats from Zenica, some of them unwilling. This is all part of the policy of reverse ethnic cleansing, of which we've heard there and elsewhere, for example, in Stupni Do. You've also heard from Witness Q, who also gave you evidence about Croats not wishing to be exchanged, and how they had to be convinced or persuaded. Can I turn from that topic, which was touched upon, to Divjak. I've already dealt with Divjak because of the mosque that we accept is not the subject of evidence, and let me come to, I think, Busovaca. Busovaca again only becomes relevant if there's any potential separation, which there isn't. This is at the centre of the facts in this case. And there are, perhaps, some other things to be said about Busovaca, particularly in relation to the Defence suggestions that life went back to normal in Busovaca at an early stage. There has, in short, been mischaracterisation of the evidence of the witnesses there. Witness A, for example, doesn't deal with the return to the quality of life at all. He deals with the way that there was a complete change in life going on in Busovaca, and he described all of the negative effects of that life, including the effects of those in the various institutions and lawful agencies who lost their jobs and positions. He deals with the sacking of Muslims and the removal of state symbols, and the taking over of radio stations. I pause there, because I should have said this earlier. Because one of the problems for the Croats in the Zenica radio station was it was the only remaining station they didn't control in the area. Witness A told you about the introduction of and necessary use of the Croatian dinar. You will find reference to -- in the documents that were produced to you, reference to the curfew, it becoming clear that the Muslims didn't have any say in these matters. They lost their rights to take part. That the HVO was leading the whole organisation of life, having abolished the Busovaca assembly and the municipal executive council. The municipal work force had to report for work immediately, but people had to place themselves under the command of the HVO. As to the suggestion that it was in some way free to people to return to work, even if they didn't join the HVO, untrue; the requirement to join applied to all, and not just to police workers. The Defence say that some workers wouldn't report, wouldn't get their jobs back if they acted without justification. Simply no support for that. You heard from Witness M saying it was clear that any Muslims that wanted to maintain a position in the government would have to become members of the HVO, and that he and other Muslims had no legal or moral powers. They just sat in their offices to pass the time. He explained how Asim Sunulpasic left the administration and believed that was for reasons of pressure and fear. He believed that the HVO wanted the Muslims working in the administration who remained simply as a bit of window-dressing for the ECMM. Witness O told you not about his own position being abolished, nor about finding a new job. He stated that he later worked at Brataslana after leaving the municipal administration position. They suggest to the Defence that he was the head of a group that was abolished. The group he headed was the executive committee itself, all part of the clear act of persecution charged in respect of Dario Kordic. The Defence would have you believe that there were two municipal departments still left headed by Muslims, and they refer to Exhibit 175.1. 175.1 may not be disputed, but what the witnesses said is as follows: Witness M, that although he was appointed to the Chief of General Administration, he had no real power in that administration, was not invited to meetings, and was not informed about what was happening. Without his knowledge, he was indeed then made a member of the HVO. More window-dressing. They say that the restructured municipal HVO government didn't require its employees to sign oaths or allegiances. The response to that is both witnesses whom I've referred to indicated they didn't sign any loyalty oaths or allegiance, but it remains implicit that that was the ultimatum they face in the order to return to work. And as to the suggestion that the community was living a relatively normal life, our response is that that is simply a failure to reflect the totality and the reality of this evidence and that these were Muslims living in fear, without rights, and without entitlements that they should otherwise have had. I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could deal with the matters in ten minutes or so, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I hope so. Amongst other topics referred to today, which, out of respect, I deal with lightly, was the so-called Ahmici report. The Chamber will recall that this was a document prepared somewhere, time unknown, made available at the end of the Blaskic case, and produced by us and shown to one witness, Colonel Stewart, not because we acknowledge it as an accurate and honest document, nor even because we accept the accuracy of its apparent date, but simply to show that if it's a false document, why would there be need to raise such a false document if things were otherwise in good order? The Chamber will recall the comments and criticisms of the report made by Colonel Stewart, and in light of the shortness of time, I won't go into it further, but the report simply doesn't fit with the events. Interestingly enough, the earlier report of Ljubesic, issued on the 16th of April, which is accepted all round as an untrue or an inaccurate document, is rather mirrored in the later report, and if one looks at the reports together, one can see, it may be argued, and we would argue if we had the time and if it was necessary, really developing cover-up. Of course, no official of the International Community was informed of or provided with this alleged nearly contemporaneous report, it first coming to light in the Blaskic Chamber and right at the end of the Blaskic case. Stupni Do. I've already dealt with that in part by dealing with aspects of Kordic's authority in Vares. It is quite clear that it can't simply be blamed on Rajic, a man for whom Kordic was shown to have an earlier intention to remove him from office, and as Mahmutovic told you, Mr. Mahmutovic told you, it's clear that in order to fire someone, that person has to work for you, and Kordic was clearly seen by, consistent with other evidence, as Rajic's superior. You heard further evidence, of course, from Sir Martin Garrod dealing with this particular area and also with the conclusions of Mr. Stutt that there was no doubt about who spoke for Central Bosnia, and he was incorporating this area within that general title or description. You will also probably have in mind from Stutt's evidence his judgement that Kordic was the third person in the military chain of command, and that's something that was also spoken of by Sir Martin Garrod himself. The alleged dismissal of three important people in the area -- and I say "alleged" advisedly -- and inquiries that follow do nothing but to show a further determination to cover things up with the light of the experience in Ahmici behind them. The evidence about Stupni Do and about Kordic's interest in that area and influence over it, including his giving orders to Rajic, Z202 as an example, fits with all the other evidence of the general policy in this area. The Chamber will have in mind, before even turning to the evidence of AO -- I accept the evidence of AO is as yet incomplete because he must come back for cross-examination. But the Chamber will recall that when the Witness AO described a decision that was made and then had to be confirmed by telephone call or by communication through the communications room, he was doing something that was an echo of what we had heard from other witnesses, and in particular the international witnesses elsewhere, where Blaskic was never able to make a final decision and had to defer to someone else. And you will also have in mind, in relation to Witness AO, how his evidence of the purpose of the Stupni Do massacre, reverse ethnic cleansing, a shock to drive the remaining Croats out, to fit in with the overarching plan, was a reflection not just of what we have now already reviewed in Zenica as a small example, but was a reflection of another witness, I think Mahmutovic, who postulated that as the real reason for the Stupni Do event. Kiseljak. Well, I've already dealt with that in part in touching on the telephone conversations that -- the telephone conversations, yes, that were overheard between Kordic and Blaskic, one in Kiseljak and one in Busovaca. And it may be worth, because I know the time is limited, just reminding you of some of the things that were said between these two people. Was in any sense Kiseljak separate from or was it simply integrated in the overall plan and scheme of things, temporarily and unhappily for the Croats, divided from Busovaca. As to the particular and critical conversation where Kordic says, "Let's burn everything. Let's hear the howitzer roar," and making his decision about Zenica. His decision to attack Zenica, only if it reacts. The Court will already have that in mind. In the same conversation he shows an interest in Fojnica, Kakanj, and Visoko. And in later conversations on the same tapes, he shows an interest, at page 13, in Vares; at page 22, an interest in Gornji Vakuf, with the remark, amongst others, "How can there be a joint command with the enemy?" And if that enemy was the Muslims, what does that tell us about his true attitude? And then at page 24 of the English transcript that I have, Kordic and Blaskic speaking together of trucks coming from Kiseljak, and Kordic congratulating Blaskic, who says, "That's aid to the brotherly people of Busovaca." And Kordic saying, "Excellent. I'll tell them tomorrow on Busovaca's radio." Everything that was going on, and is evidenced as going on, it reflects the overall joint plan to which I'll return very briefly in a moment. I can deal with the Cerkez arguments compactly presented both in writing and today briefly. All the arguments you've heard today have been arguments on weight of the evidence, as I understand it. Our brief has dealt with that. It's dealt with the time problem, not that the problem is something that can be dealt with on this indictment. Not that the time issue can be dealt with on this indictment, because it's a non-separable count. It's worth bearing in mind that Cerkez's personal presence at various locations is not required. It has to be brought to mind, it's him and those he commands for whom he bears responsibility. And so even if it be the case that some particular location is shown not to have been visited with him, not to the point. He referred to, my friend Mr. Kovacic, a couple of lists produced, I think, by the BiH military police, detailing offenders, several of whom are shown to have been members of the Viteska Brigade, including the killing of Trako and the cinema rapist. The evidence we've produced or that has been produced is going to show that this was an active man elsewhere, is relevant going to show that he is not a desk-bound commander, but that is all. He is an active commander in the field. And so I return to our final position, brief as I have attempted to be. It's important for the Chamber, perhaps, just to remind itself that this starts as a widespread plan. And you can look at the Tudjman meeting setting out the dual-track approach, the problems with the Muslims. You can look at Valenta's book, which is by no means as innocent in effect as the Defence would have you believe in their brief. Yes, he may not have spoken in writing of violence, he may not have had violence in mind. One doesn't know, at the time he wrote it. But the book is written at a time when people got on comparatively well together. And it speaks of the compulsory movement of a sector of the population identified by ethnicity. What effect is that ever likely to have on those involved? And of course to a significant extent we have to look at not just what people say and do, but the setting in which they do it. You have asked to attend to the perceptions of appearances by Mr. Kordic on the television. The perceptions may have been grey. Anybody making the broadcasts that were made, having the effects that would be had on an ethnically identified part of the community, would have known that. And they don't have to go the whole hog, in the vernacular, and spell out in anticipation that violence was a necessary and inevitable part of what was going to happen. So it starts as a joint plan, which the defendant, Kordic, is, in effect, one of the authors in an early stage, in there with Tudjman and so on. And thereafter, when there are meetings organised, you will see from the documents, and we needn't go through them all now, that every municipality is involved; invitations to every municipality, everyone summoned. The plan starts as an area-wide. The Central Bosnia-wide plan continues in that way, and as the evidence with its various similar features, as between one attack and another so compellingly reveals, executed on an area-wide, on a Central Bosnia-wide basis. And for that the evidence shows there is no politician more important than Kordic. No one else is identified as the person who would be wielding the political power. No other politician is shown as having the political authority at direct and discrete incidents that he did. And the Chamber will have in mind that, of course, with the access to documents these defendants may have, if documents either fully identified Kordic's role, as opposed to the multiplicity of roles that his titles revealed, you would have seen it, a fortiori, if there was any document going to show who else lay behind what happened. We note that it does not appear to be the case any more that the international armed conflict is challenged. We draw to your respectful attention that although we've reviewed this matter swiftly as we've been able to, facing the Defence motion that we did substantially on the basis of oral testimony, a full and final analysis of this case will, of course, have to include careful analysis of the documents. For, in the case of political leadership, there is always going to be a lot to be divined from and probably painstakingly divined from the documents. We go back to the formalities as to Annex 1. Our position is as I said it was. But we would, of course, ask for the position to be deferred as to striking items out, because the document, although I hope it's complete, hasn't been finally checked. Particularly, it hasn't been checked for any entries that might be supported by documents. Can I help any further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. I'll do my best to respond on the fly because these arguments have not been made in writing. The standard of review. There's a lot been said on that. I am not going to add too much. Apparently, it seems to be the Prosecution's position that any evidence, any evidence at all, satisfies the requirement of the reasonable Trial Chamber standard that's being articulated today. A mere scintilla would be enough, and thrust upon the defendant the burden of going forward. We submit that that's not the test. The principle seems to be that it's enough to introduce evidence that crimes occurred in a village such as Rotilj or Tulica, as I have stated, and that's sufficient for purposes of passing muster, but it's not sufficient unless there's some proven connection with Mr. Kordic. If there is some proven connection that his subordinates, people over whom he had command responsibility, were responsible for these crimes, and there is none with respect to those two villages and, we would submit, for a variety of other locations for the reasons that I've previously stated. With respect to the civil role that the Prosecution adverted to, this is not a civil case. The rights of defendants in criminal cases are not applicable in a civil case. Rule 98 bis is applicable to this case. With respect to the motion for adjudicated facts, we will respond to that in writing as directed by the Trial Chamber and within the time limit that the Trial Chamber has requested us to respond. With respect to Mr. Kordic, once again the Prosecution has indeed proved that in many locales there were crimes. They've also failed to prove, with respect to many locales, that there were any crimes at all. But even in those locales where crimes have been or evidence of crimes has been adduced, there is little or no connection that those crimes had anything to do with Mr. Kordic. The claim is made, "Well, he must have had power because he never disclaimed it." But the failure to disclaim you had power when the question was never asked does not equal the actual possession of that power, and I merely refer the Court once again to the three witnesses who actually did ask the question, Jean-Mark Lanthier; Major Jennings, page 8995. "Are you the HVO commander?" he asked Mr. Kordic. And he acknowledged that Mr. Kordic said, "No." He asked the question; he got the response. I'm not going to belabour all of the extensive recitation of the evidence that we've put in our brief where conclusions were made, very hand-waving type of conclusions, well, he was a man of power, he must have had some sort of power. No one was able to provide any details, no one. And that's not going to pass muster in a criminal case, we would submit. Now, Count 1, "and" means "or." No, it doesn't. "And" means "and." We didn't plead the count, the Prosecution did, and they -- it's been -- the amended indictment has been amended, obviously, and all you have to do is look at paragraph 37(J) of the amendment indictment and the word "and" is there. It is a conjunctive requirement. Not a disjunctive, conjunctive. And they haven't proved that there was persecution throughout all of the area of the municipalities adverted to in the amended indictment. It may assist the Trial Chamber, I didn't have my copy of the amended indictment with me when the question arose this morning, but the actual municipalities that are specifically identified in the amended indictment are identified in paragraph 5, Your Honours. And as I said, as to about 24 of those municipalities, there is no evidence. And we are told today, for example, that there are areas that are outside the indictment, such as Mostar, where terrible things were happening too. Well, as you can see from paragraph 5, Mostar is actually in the indictment. But even if there were awful things happening in Mostar, there is absolutely no evidence that they had anything to do with Mr. Kordic, and the same is true with respect to most of the other information. Now, with respect to the persecution, the generalised persecution claims made about Mr. Kordic and the speeches that he made very early on, in September of 1992, December of 1991, consider this Your Honours: Consider the huge amount of videotape evidence that's been provided to you and transcript evidence by the Prosecution. Where also the huge amount of print media exhibits that have been introduced by the Prosecution, there is not one that they can point to, not one videotape or print media article where the Prosecution can say that Mr. Kordic is making ethnically disparaging comments, rabble-rousing, table pounding, foaming at the mouth, inciting violence. There simply isn't one. The evidence is before Your Honours to see for yourself and assess for yourselves what he actually said as opposed to fractured recollections years later of what he supposedly said, and the most vivid example was the one mentioned by Mr. Smith. It's Witness AQ. Witness AQ was brought to this Trial Chamber for one purpose, and that is to say there were two speeches given by Kordic supposedly on the night of April 15th. One that was in Exhibit Z665, which is a videotape that she was showed, and the another, a different speech for which there is no videotape, where extreme comments were made, where an incitement of violence supposedly occurred. And I'm sure the Trial Chamber recalls, as I do, that many attempts were made to persuade Witness AQ that the video statement was different from the speech that she remembered, and she said no, it's the same speech. And indeed the Presiding Judge specifically asked that question and she confirmed the information; same speech. So we would just refer the Court to the videotapes and the newspaper articles, the print media articles. Those are the best evidence of what the man said. He's shown on videotape saying what he says and you can assess it yourself. There is simply nothing of a discriminatory, persecutory nature there at all. Now, with respect to the particular villages mentioned by the Prosecution, it's refreshing to find that Travnik and Fojnica are out of the villages as to which specific crimes are mentioned. With respect to Rotilj and Tulica, as I say, no connection with Dario Kordic. With respect to Zepce, Your Honours, absolutely no connection with Dario Kordic. Notwithstanding the reference to the testimony of Colonel Stutt, Witness AD, and Sir Martin Garrod. None of those witnesses testified that Mr. Kordic had the slightest power or influence in Zepce, and indeed Colonel Stutt testified to precisely the reverse. There is quite simply no evidence that Mr. Kordic had influence in Zepce or let alone that his subordinates or people who were subordinates to him in some quasi-military or civilian sense or any people for whom he might be held to have superior responsibility committed the crimes in Zepce. With respect to the Zenica shelling, you can read our submission on that. I have nothing to add to it. With respect to Divjak, I think that there's a concession that Count 43 has to be dismissed because there is no evidence of any destruction of institutions dedicated to religion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The evidence is, I believe, and I stand to be corrected by the Trial Chamber, but there were only four Muslims in the Busovaca government, none of them were required to sign loyalty oaths. There is no evidence that any Muslim representative of the Busovaca government was ever required to sign a loyalty oath or did so. Now, Witness M, he didn't lose his job. He didn't sign a loyalty job. He continued on in his job. I think Nijaz Neslanovic testified she continued on in her job. Witness O, his job was eliminated but he wasn't throw into penury, he took up his old job at the factory --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- north-west of Busovaca in the town. He continued to work; he continued to get paid. He wasn't required to sign any loyalty oaths or anything like that. With respect to the allegations of reverse ethnic cleansing, I have to confess there I greet those with some skepticism. It seems to be the proposition that whenever Bosnian Muslims are pushed out of their homes that's the fault of the Croats. Whenever Bosnian Croats are pushed out of their homes that's the fault of the Bosnian Croats too. We would submit that the evidence simply does not sustain that charge of reverse ethnic cleansing and the ECMM documents pretty much affirmatively prove it. With respect to the Ahmici report, Your Honour, I'm not going to say anything other than that. The Prosecution says, "Well, it's a cover-up." But not by Kordic. It wasn't Kordic that introduced this document into evidence, it was the Prosecution. There is no evidence that Kordic had any role in any cover-up and there is no contention that the May the 10th, 1993 order issued by Colonel Blaskic was in any way dummied up or a phoney order. With respect to Stupni Do, I have to say there is no evidence of Mr. Kordic's influence in Stupni Do. In fact, the Court will no doubt recall Witness AD's graphic testimony to the effect that Mr. Kordic appeared sometimes to be out of touch with things that were even going on in the Busovaca-Vitez pocket, a piece of testimony that was actually confirmed by Colonel Stutt, who said that Mr. Kordic was more for the big picture type of things and really didn't get involved in the nitty-gritty operational matters of the type that Colonel Blaskic would get involved in. He also testified rather graphically to the extensive geographic separation between Vares and the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, and there is no evidence that Mr. Kordic was ever seen in Vares at any time in 1993, and the reliance on orders signed in 1992, Your Honour, I think is rather unconvincing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the inferences that the Prosecution seeks to compress out of the dubious testimony of Witness AO, even if it weren't -- I have about three more minutes, Your Honour. With respect to Witness AO, the inferences that the Prosecution seeks to extrude from his testimony are simply not there. Even if you take everything that this witness said as true, which we would submit would be absolutely unjustified, but even if you could assume that this witness were worthy of any credit, he doesn't establish to whom Rajic spoke when he went to the communications command centre, as he says. He did not say that Rajic spoke to Kordic. He merely mentioned that either the name of Kordic or Petkovic cropped up or was mentioned in some undefined context after he returned from the communications centre. And that's it. That's as good as it gets. There is no contention that Rajic was in communication with Kordic. And the best evidence, Your Honour, of who commanded whom is just 11 days before Stupni Do the ECMM document, referred to in our brief, actually shows Kordic [sic] issuing an order to Rajic relating to road communications and improvements. And that's in the contemporaneously-generated ECMM documents. And that's, as you would expect, in the military chain of command in the ordinary course. With respect to Kiseljak -- I'm sorry, the transcript says the evidence actually shows Kordic issuing an order to Rajic. It should say Blaskic. That's what I thought I said. Blaskic issuing an order to Rajic relating to road improvements. Apparently, he had refused to make some road improvements that UNPROFOR had requested, and Blaskic intervened and directed him to do precisely that. That was on October 12th, just a few days before Stupni Do. Kiseljak, I've made my points with respect to that. With respect to the international armed conflict comment made by the Prosecution, that it doesn't appear to be challenged, it absolutely is challenged. And we will respond within, once again, the time period that was required by the Trial Chamber. I think next week and next Friday is the date that the Trial Chamber directed us to respond. And we will. Let me just finish up by saying that the Presiding Judge made a comment early on in this case saying, "I hope this isn't going to be a case about politics." And it has largely turned out to be a case about politics, unfortunately. But institutions are not on trial in this case. President Tudjman, now deceased, is not on trial in this case. Mr. Kordic is. And it's what he said and what he did that the Court should focus on. Now, the Prosecution has, as we've said, taken its best shot. They have had 11 months to do so. I think the Court has been extraordinarily generous in providing 11 months and 150 witnesses, including transcript and affidavit witnesses, for them to put on evidence of some crime committed by Mr. Kordic or some connection that he has some superior responsibility that he has. They have introduced not merely a mountain of documents, but a mountain range of documents, in the thousands, I believe. This Prosecution -- this criminal proceeding has been five, six years in the making, Your Honours. And it's time now for the Court to take a look at the evidence. And we would suggest that, first of all, there's been no proof beyond a reasonable doubt of any criminal culpability on Mr. Kordic's part. And, secondly, no reasonable Trial Chamber could conclude that based upon this evidence there is sufficient evidence to convict Mr. Kordic of any of the specific crimes alleged in the amended indictment, even where there is some evidence, as opposed to those municipalities where there is none. And so we merely ask the Court to apply Rule 98 bis, as did the Trial Chamber in Jelisic, and reach the appropriate decision, which is an acquittal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall be really very, very brief. It is so late, and of course there is not too much sense to comment on all comments of my learned colleague. But let me proceed in Croatian; it's much easier for me. [Interpretation] We have the same confusion, the same time. There are no subordinate persons to Cerkez in 1992, and I am giving a very rough definition of this type. Throughout these proceedings in the Prosecution case, no argument was presented for Count 2. Nothing was said about his participation in it, personally. And he cannot be charged in his superior capacity until he was appointed the commander of the brigade. That is as far as Busovaca is concerned. Cerkez became the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade commander and was physically in Novi Travnik. He was in the staff. He was not a commander. He was on Mount Vlasic. And there are no charges that he did anything in Novi Travnik. Why? Again, we are facing a problem of time. Because nothing happened in Novi Travnik that is incriminating. After October 1992, a truce was reached and a status quo was established. At the very end of 1992, Cerkez is in Novi Travnik and then nothing was going on there. We heard nothing. We heard at a very end that a witness said that his brother was killed there. And it was clearly a common crime. It had nothing to do with the HVO soldiers. This is why I insist so much to define the territory, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, Vitez. In Vitez, as is since -- after April 1993, that is a different situation, and we can focus on that. I want to point out one more thing. Perhaps I was not clear enough, and it is my fault. The lists of war criminals produced by witness Rebihic, which I believe are important, I did not mention in order to say that Cerkez is not guilty because he is not mentioned in any of these lists. It is something else. Cerkez, obviously, was not personally responsible, according to the BiH intelligence sources, that is the witness Rebihic. And Mr. Rebihic had Mr. Cerkez before his eyes, so to speak, for a very long time. And Witness Rebihic did not compile his list on a legal basis. He did not have any legal basis in mind; having in mind a theory of superior responsibility. He was a practically illiterate man. It would have been impossible. So I don't think that anybody should convince anybody about that. Now, whether he put -- somebody else was involved in this, that is a separate matter. I think that he was just trying to hunt down certain men. At that time, the Statute of the Tribunal did not exist. Even if it did, he would not have known about it also. The murder in the hotel, the Vukadinovic case, that was again May 1992. Vukadinovic was not his man. He was part of the military police, the alleged killer. This was the man who was on guard duty at that time. Then we also have the municipal headquarters in Vitez, the head of this -- the staff is Marijan Skopljak. The documents proved this. So, if in 1992 anybody committed any crime in Vitez, this cannot be ascribed to Mario Cerkez, because he was not in a position of authority at that time. He is only responsible for himself, personally. There is no evidence as to his involvement in any crime throughout 1992; that is, until he became the commander of Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, which was in late February 1993. And later on he became the commander of the Vitez Brigade. Only from that moment on can he be potentially responsible, liable, but first we have to determine that some subordinate of his committed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Kovacic. What are you asking for, what is it exactly? As regards the issue that has been submitted to us, as regards the application of Rule 98 bis, what is it exactly that you are asking for? What are you asking this Trial Chamber to do? Are you asking us not to look at each and every act committed until February of 1993? I am not sure what it is you are asking for, in terms of Rule 98 bis. In practical terms, what does what you are saying have to do with the application of Rule 98 bis? Please explain yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I am trying to be very brief, and obviously I am making mistakes here. Your Honours, my submission is, and I believe that a fair interpretation of 98 bis, I believe that the Trial Chamber has the right to dismiss even parts of charges within individual charges. I am going a step further, and I submit that the Trial Chamber specifically as an example in the point 2, persecution, has the right to dismiss charges for the period from April 1992 to April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. Kovacic. But doesn't it all amount to the following: You want us to modify again the indictment. Isn't it what you are asking for? Because Article -- sorry, Rule 98 bis asks the Judges to make sure whether or not it is possible for them to enter a judgement of acquittal. And they are trying to see whether or not the evidence is sufficient for them to enter a judgement of acquittal. And you are, in fact, I think, asking if part of the indictment can be done away with, deleted. Aren't you asking for a further amendment of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not asking for an amendment of the indictment, because that would reverse the whole process and the confirmation of the indictment, so on and so forth. I am requesting that the Trial Chamber rule on a part of a count, at least, because at this time the Trial Chamber can dismiss the entire count. But -- and if a whole count can be dismissed at this point, or acquit on a particular count, then the Trial Chamber can certainly acquit on a part of a count, in which case the whole indictment would be narrowed. And the acquittal can be effected on the parts which did not rise to the standard of primae facie. And, in our submission, and let me just stay with this example, Count 2, that no evidence was offered which would lead to consideration of guilt on Count 2, as in reference to the Busovaca and Novi Travnik municipalities, because no evidence has been offered that would rise above the standard of primae facie. And this is what we believe is within the right of the Trial Chamber to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider these matters and give our decision next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: May I just raise one very brief issue, Your Honour. There is an ex parte in camera motion that is pending before the Court, in the event that the Court reaches a decision adverse from that, which we are urging today has some urgency. And there are outstanding applications that have been made that relate to the same matters, which we would appreciate a decision on, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
